summary: Defines a management database module for monitoring network services, usable on its own for simple applications. It also serves as a building block alongside application-specific monitoring. It replaces RFC 1565 and was replaced by RFC 2788.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a standard way for a manager to check on programs that give services over the network, like a health chart for each one.

subtitle: Standard objects for monitoring network application status and connections.

tldr.problem: Network administrators need a standard way to monitor the health, status, and activity of network service applications such as mail servers and directory services, but lower-layer network monitoring alone does not provide application-specific visibility.
tldr.mechanism: This MIB defines tables and objects that track each monitored application's operational status, connection counts, activity timestamps, and associations with other applications, allowing management stations to query a common interface.
tldr.outcome: Operators gained a standard foundation for application-layer monitoring that could be extended by application-specific MIBs; it was superseded by RFC 2788.

facts.label: Operational states
facts.value: up, down, halted, congested, restarting, quiescing

today: RFC 2248 is Proposed Standard status and has been obsoleted by RFC 2788, which refines and extends the monitoring model. Modern network management systems use SNMP MIBs based on this framework to monitor applications and services.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2248 defines the Network Services Monitoring MIB, a management information base for monitoring network service applications via SNMP. Network service applications such as mail servers and directory services run on hosts and require visibility into their operation—not just the network connectivity below them, but their own status and activity.

This MIB is designed to be used on its own for simple applications and as a foundation that can be extended by application-specific MIBs (for example, mail transfer agent (MTA) or directory service agent (DSA) MIBs) that add additional monitoring for their particular protocol details. The MIB provides read-only access focused on operational status, load monitoring, and problem detection rather than configuration control.
sections.plainLanguage: This tells you how to ask a network service 'are you running, how many people are connected to you, and when did anyone last talk to you'. Different services can add their own details on top.

sections.title: The Application Table
sections.content:
The core of the MIB is the applTable, which holds one entry for each monitored network service application on the system. Each entry is indexed by an integer applIndex.

Basic identity fields include applName (the application's self-chosen name), applVersion (vendor-provided version string), and applDirectoryName (a Distinguished Name linking to X.500 directory entries for static information).

applUptime records when the application was last started (relative to the system's uptime), and applOperStatus indicates the current operational state: up (running and available), down (not available), halted (running but not available), congested (can't accept more connections), restarting (temporarily unavailable), or quiescing (shutting down gracefully).
sections.plainLanguage: For each service, you store its name, version, when it started, and whether it is running, stuck, overloaded, or shutting down. You also note a directory entry for more details.

sections.title: Connection and Activity Monitoring
sections.content:
applInboundAssociations and applOutboundAssociations are current counts of active connections: inbound where the application is the responder (someone connected to it), and outbound where it is the initiator (it connected to someone).

applAccumulatedInboundAssociations and applAccumulatedOutboundAssociations are lifetime counters since the application started, providing a measure of load history.

applLastInboundActivity and applLastOutboundActivity record when the application last had any incoming or outgoing connection, helping detect stuck or dormant services. applRejectedInboundAssociations and applFailedOutboundAssociations count connection rejections and failures, indicating problems or overload.

applLastChange marks when the application entered its current operational status, useful for tracking how long it has been in its present state.
sections.plainLanguage: You count the connections right now, the total lifetime connections, when someone last tried to reach the service, and how many connections it rejected. This shows how busy it is and how healthy it seems.

sections.title: Tracking Connections
sections.content:
The assocTable provides detailed information about individual associations (connections) of each application. It is indexed by both applIndex and assocIndex, linking each connection to its parent application.

assocRemoteApplication names the other system involved in the association, using domain names, IP addresses, or X.500 distinguished names depending on the protocol. assocApplicationProtocol is an object identifier indicating the protocol in use: either an IANA-registered OID or a derived OID based on port number (for example, {applTCPProtoID 25} for SMTP).

assocApplicationType classifies the connection as ua-initiator (a user agent initiating a request), ua-responder (a user agent using the service), peer-initiator (a peer server initiating), or peer-responder (a peer server responding). assocDuration records when the association started.
sections.plainLanguage: For each active connection, you store who you are talking to, what protocol you are using, whether you or they started it, and how long it has been active.

sections.title: Design and Extensibility
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that this MIB provides common ground for any network service application. Application-specific MIBs (such as those for mail servers or directory services) are expected to extend it with additional objects relevant to their protocols.

The MIB deliberately keeps the scope narrow: it does not manage host resources, application configuration, or request-level details (such as querying the status of a specific email message). These responsibilities are left to the Host Resources MIB, future application MIBs, and application-specific extensions respectively.

Configuration information about the application itself may be stored in a directory service, referenced by applDirectoryName or the applURL field (added in RFC 2248). This design separates the simple, read-only monitoring baseline from application-specific or directory-based configuration details.
sections.plainLanguage: This MIB is a foundation: it gives you the basics (is it running, how loaded is it). Specific services add their own measurements. Configuration lives in the directory, not here.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 2248 offers read-only access, so it cannot be used to actively attack a system. However, the MIB does expose information about the existence, type, and configuration of applications on a host, which could reveal vulnerabilities or inform targeted attacks.

Additionally, the MIB provides passive data about network usage patterns that could be analyzed to understand traffic flows, user behavior, or system load. Access to monitoring data should be restricted according to organizational security policies, typically through SNMP authentication and access controls (SNMPv3 security or community strings in SNMPv1/v2c).
sections.plainLanguage: Since this only shows information (you cannot change anything with it), it cannot directly attack the system. But the information it reveals about what services are running and how busy they are could help someone plan an attack, so you should control who can read it.
